newsitem.title: INDIA: Anti-Miss World activists spurn offer of talks.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Miss World activists spurn offer of talks.

text.p: Miss World organiser Julia Morley said on Saturday leaders of a militant Indian womens' group threatening to wreck the show by staging human torch suicide protests had spurned her offer of talks.

"We've offered our hand to these people to come and see what Miss World is all about. But their blind prejudice is very difficult to overcome," Morley, president of Miss World Organisation told Reuters in Bangalore.
"We are not interested in holding talks with them. Let the organisers first stop the show." Kinay Narayan Shishikala, firebrand leader of the Mahila Jagran Samiti told Reuters.
The protesters say the beauty pageant demeans women and represents an invasion of of Indian culture.
A 25-year old man killed himself by self-immolation on Thursday in Madurai, some 432 kilometres (270 miles) away from Bangalore, the southern city hosting Miss World.
The death sent shudders through Morley and husband Eric, who founded a show that has become an annual fixture of television programmers worldwide.
It also raised fears of copy-cat suicides to come.
While the controversy raged the 88 contestants went through reheasals again on Saturday.
Their next public outing will be on Sunday for the Miss Photogenic phase of the contest, to be held in the outskirts of India's "Garden City".
Around two billion television viewers in 115 countries are expected to watch Miss World being crowned on November 23.
Security forces will be watching the 20,000 people inside the Chinnaswamy cricket stadium for final night.
Members of the Mahila Jagran Samiti have threatened to infiltrate the crowd, take cyanide pills to lessen the pain and set light to their silk saris to die in flames.
Because of cultural differences the alarm is greater among non-Indians about the lengths that "fanatics" will go to grab attention, Julia Morley said.
"For me it is horrific. But local people just shrug their shoulders," Julia Morley said.
She was saddened and angered by the suicide in Madurai, but said Miss World was not going to fold up and leave.
And the Mahila Jagran Smaiti is holding its threat in abeyance, while waiting for a court ruling on its petition to ban the show.
"We will decide on a course of action after the judgement," Shishikala said.

A judge is expected to make his decision on Monday, and if he turns down the petition, the Karanataka state government in Bangalore will be free to call in around 2,000 paramilitary officers to help safeguard the event.
All previous attempts to block the pageant through the courts have failed.
Pramila Nesargi, a legislator for the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) who has moved four petitions in court, also saw little point to talks with the organisers.
"I don't see any purpose in having a meeting with them. We believe strongly that such shows are an assault on our culture. It is still not too late for them to call it off," she said.

Julia Morley said politicians and extremist groups were trying to sensationalise the event for their own ends, and the local people in Bangalore have welcomed Miss World and are upset by the bad publicity generated by a minority.

Hometown girl, Vidhisha Pavate, a top model who now graces Paris catwalks recently told Reuters: "The arguments are silly. We faced the British invasion and the Moghul rule. One pageant lasting two hours cannot affect our culture."
